analysis.one_liner: Makes hardrock mining companies pay royalties and cleanup costs for metals taken from federal land.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2022 with six Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and expired with the 117th Congress in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Mining Law of 1872, anyone can stake a claim on federal land, buy the land outright for almost nothing, and remove gold, copper, and other hardrock minerals without paying the government a cent in royalties. This bill would end those outright land sales going forward, charge mining companies a royalty of 5 to 8 percent of their income from the minerals, add a 1 to 3 percent cleanup fee, and require permits, reclamation bonds, and tribal consultation before mining begins. The money would fund cleanup of tens of thousands of abandoned mines that leach acid and toxic metals into streams. The bill never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently get nothing when companies extract billions of dollars of gold, copper, and other metals from public land; people who live near mines and abandoned mine sites, whose water is threatened by acid mine drainage; and tribes, who would get formal consultation before mining near culturally significant land.

how_it_helps.text: Charges mining companies a federal royalty of at least 5 percent and up to 8 percent of gross income on minerals produced from federal land, something the 1872 Mining Law never required.

Prohibits the government from issuing patents — deeds converting a mining claim into private land — unless the application was filed before September 30, 1994, ending the practice of buying public land for roughly $5 an acre.

Imposes a reclamation fee of 1 to 3 percent of production value to build a fund for cleaning up abandoned hardrock mines, and requires operators to post bonds sufficient to restore land and water before any mining begins.

Requires exploration and mining permits with plans to prevent acid mine drainage, public notice and comment, quarterly inspections, and consultation with tribes before any permit affecting tribal land or culturally significant areas is issued.

Establishes civil penalties of up to $25,000 per day for false records, stolen minerals, or refusal to pay royalties, plus criminal fines up to $50,000 and two years' imprisonment for willful violations.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies, which would pay royalties, cleanup fees, annual claim fees, land use fees, and reclamation bonds; some of those costs could be passed through to buyers of metals used in batteries and electronics. Small claim holders with ten or fewer claims are exempted from the new maintenance fees.

drawbacks.text: Existing mines with approved operations plans already producing in commercial quantities are exempt from the royalty, so the new revenue would apply only to future or newly approved operations.

Royalties, fees, and permit requirements raise the cost and lead time of domestic mining at a moment when demand for copper, lithium, and other battery and renewable-energy minerals is rising; the bill itself includes a royalty-relief provision for operators who can show production would not happen without a reduction, an acknowledgment of that risk.
The annual $200 claim maintenance fee and new land use fees add recurring costs, though the fee is waived for claim holders with ten or fewer claims who have performed required assessment work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits are concrete and large: the federal government collects revenue it now forgoes entirely, abandoned mine sites that poison water get a dedicated cleanup fund, and operators must post bonds so taxpayers are not left holding reclamation bills. The chief real cost is that higher fees and fuller permitting could raise the price or slow the supply of domestically mined minerals for clean energy. The grandfathering of existing mines significantly limits near-term revenue, making the bill's fiscal benefit smaller than a full reform would be.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in April 2022, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Martin Heinrich introduced the bill on April 26, 2022, joined by six Democratic cosponsors; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote — the referral was the last recorded action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies are better off: the 1872 Mining Law remains in force, so they continue to extract minerals from federal land royalty-free, hold claims indefinitely with only nominal fees, and carry no federal reclamation bonding requirement. Taxpayers continue to absorb the cost of abandoned mine pollution beyond what recent infrastructure funding covers.

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; bill sponsor

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Bennet, Merkley, Luján, Booker, Wyden, Markey)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the referral was its last recorded action.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Mining companies and trade associations holding federal claims
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal royalties, fees, and new permitting requirements on hardrock mining.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there are no roll calls to break down; all seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, no Republicans signed on, and the Democratic-led committee that never acted was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, copper, lithium, uranium, and other locatable minerals)
industries.note: Under the 1872 Mining Law these companies extract minerals from federal land with no royalty and can patent claims into private ownership; the bill would impose a 5-8 percent royalty, a 1-3 percent cleanup fee, permit requirements, and reclamation bonds, ending a subsidy that ordinary taxpayers currently cover. Existing producing mines are grandfathered out of the royalty, softening the near-term hit.

industries.industry: Claim holders and mining claim speculators
industries.note: The bill ends new patents, requires a $200 annual maintenance fee per claim, and voids claims not used exclusively for mineral activities, targeting holders who keep claims off the market as land or investment rather than mining. Holders with ten or fewer claims are exempted from the maintenance fee.

industries.industry: Abandoned mine reclamation and water treatment
industries.note: A 1-3 percent reclamation fee would fund cleanup of abandoned hardrock mines that leach acid and heavy metals into public waters, work that today falls on taxpayers and downstream communities.
